title: Inside a real UFO contact movement: Meditation, laser pointers, and wilderness retreats
excerpt: An anthropologist studies CE-5, a movement whose members use meditation and laser pointers to attempt contact with UFOs.
content:
While governments release more files on unidentified aerial phenomena, one researcher is studying a very different piece of the UFO puzzle. His focus: the people who believe they've already made contact. An anthropology professor has spent years documenting a movement whose members use meditation, laser pointers, and group rituals in organized attempts to reach extraterrestrial visitors.

Shayne Dahl, an assistant professor of anthropology and archaeology, has researched a movement known as Close Encounters of the Fifth Kind, or CE-5. Small communities within that movement travel together to remote wilderness locations. There, members combine meditation, visualization techniques, and laser pointers in coordinated efforts to initiate contact with UFOs and their potential occupants.

Born from curiosity

Interest in the intersection of religion and UFOs first grabbed Dahl's attention back in 2017, sparked by a New York Times article on the subject. Years later, he began interviewing CE-5 participants directly, eventually developing a full research project examining the movement.

Participants' core claim is straightforward: they believe they can actually establish contact. That claim, along with the elaborate rituals built around it, struck Dahl as worth studying through the lens of religious anthropology rather than dismissing outright.

Not proving aliens exist

A firm line separates what this research does and doesn't attempt to answer. The work isn't intended to promote UFO disclosure efforts, nor does it try to determine whether extraterrestrial visitors are actually present on Earth.

Understanding how people respond to the mere possibility of contact is the actual goal, according to Dahl. He has described his own role simply as an anthropologist trying to piece together a genuinely puzzling social phenomenon. That's a different task from attempting to adjudicate its underlying truth.

Coining "techno-shamanism"

The term "techno-shamanism" is how Dahl has come to describe what he's observed within CE-5 communities. He frames the movement as a genuine, functioning form of religious practice built around modern technology and cosmic belief. He published his findings in an August article for The Conversation, and plans to expand the work into a full academic essay later this year.

Growing UFO-related disclosure activity in the United States has drawn Dahl's attention, and he has become increasingly interested in how ordinary people process that uncertainty. A recurring theme surfaces across CE-5 communities, he said: a desire for what he calls cosmic belonging, a sense of connection to something larger than Earth itself.

Determining whether extraterrestrial life is actually visiting the planet falls outside his own area of expertise, in Dahl's view. That question is better left to scientists or government investigators, he said. His focus remains squarely on the humans doing the searching, not on what, if anything, they might eventually find.
